prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints tied to asset values amplify and propagate shocks, and for establishing a dynamic theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identify a specific dynamic mechanism: borrowing limits tied to the value of collateral assets turn temporary shocks into persistent, amplified fluctuations. This is a conceptual discovery rather than a tool. It became the base for the later literature on financial frictions, intermediary balance sheets and macroprudential policy, and it shaped how the 2008 crisis was analysed. The contribution is cleanly attributable to a two-author paper, and about thirty years of theoretical, quantitative and empirical follow-up mean the Committee is not judging it prematurely. I have also moved from my opening three-name proposal to two names. The colleagues who ranked B007 highly (Boppart, Hassler, Enflo, Friberg, Teorell, Andersson) all proposed the pair. They argue that the accelerator strand is entangled with Bernanke's 2022 recognition, and I find that persuasive. The pair gives the tightest and most defensible attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig on banks and financial crises. The Committee could see financial frictions as already recognised, with Kiyotaki-Moore as a refinement. The mechanism is also more securely established in theory and quantitative models than through clean empirical identification of collateral channels. Narrowing to two names leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose work on the accelerator and on intermediary frictions was influential. B007 is also a narrower body of work than the New Keynesian framework in B012 or the trade framework in B026. Cleaner attribution does not by itself make a discovery more important, and I try not to let it count as merit.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B007 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He sees the collateral mechanism as fundamental and the credit as a clear two-author contribution. He treats the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator as overlapping with the 2022 prize, so he leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist.
responses.response: I agree and have revised my opening view accordingly. I had added Gertler for his intermediary-friction work, including the line with Kiyotaki. On reflection that is a related but separable contribution, and including him blurs the discovery and invites the 2022 overlap objection. I would still stress that the Committee should not read the pair as a dismissal of Gertler's record. His claims are separate and could be judged on their own, including under B012. I read the maturity point the same way Boppart does, since the evidence base now spans three decades.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B012 first. He argues that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are the clearest originators of the core elements of the New Keynesian framework, that its policy impact is very large, and that the Taylor rule is more a rule of thumb than a deep theoretical result. He ranks B007 second.
responses.response: I accept that the policy and scientific footprint of B012 is at least as large as B007's, and I do not think B007 dominates on impact. My reservation concerns attribution and the post-2021 empirical record. Eight credited names cover distinct strands (pricing, rules, policy theory, estimation, empirical Phillips curves). Whichever triple is chosen leaves out contributions such as Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans, Gali and Smets-Wouters that were central to making the framework usable. I share his view that the Taylor rule weighs less than Calvo or Woodford, which makes the three-way split harder, not easier. I therefore keep B012 as an alternative rather than my preferred part. I also note that his own ranking puts B007 second with the same two-name attribution I now propose.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first. She argues that Melitz (2003) and Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple transformed the theory and measurement of gains from trade, that the framework has more than twenty years of confirmation, and that it is distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize.
responses.response: I find this a strong case, and B026 is a close alternative for me (my opening rank was fifth). The breadth of support across the Committee is notable, though I do not treat support counts as scientific merit. My reservations are about credit: Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum made parallel empirical and quantitative contributions that this ballot does not credit, and Helpman's credit is also spread across the separate trade-politics line. I would want those attribution questions settled before treating a Melitz-Helpman pair as clean. If the Committee judges that Melitz's originating role makes the pair sufficiently clear, B026 is better than my preferred part on breadth of influence.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B001 first. She sees law and finance as a durable empirical programme but flags concerns about replicability, revised measures such as the anti-director index, and the overlap with the 2024 institutions prize.
responses.response: The influence of law and finance is real, and I ranked it second. Her replicability concern is the main reason I keep it below B007. The causal reading of legal origins has been contested more heavily than the collateral-amplification mechanism has been challenged as a mechanism. Excluding Vishny also costs attribution under the three-name cap. The 2024 overlap is a fair additional concern. I would not treat it as disqualifying, but with contested identification and a four-author attribution problem I prefer B007.

uncertainties: How much weight the Committee should give the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises when judging whether Kiyotaki-Moore is a distinct discovery.
Whether the Committee prefers the narrower collateral-constraint pair or a broader macro-finance framing that would reopen the Gertler and Gilchrist claims.
How strongly the collateral channel is identified empirically, as opposed to theoretically and quantitatively.
Whether B012 or B026 deserves priority on breadth of influence, given that the attribution problems in each (diffuse credit in B012, uncredited parallel contributors in B026) are unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: From the supplied profile: I have co-authored with Timo Boppart (co-opted member), including the 2018 Myrdal Prize article, and have long-term co-authorship with John Hassler (chair). Both rank B007 or B012 highly and are cited above. I have co-authored with Anthony Smith, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood, Hercowitz, Tsyvinski and Olovsson, none of whom is a credited name on B007. My own field is macroeconomics, adjacent to the macro-finance topic of B007, and I have no personal connection to Kiyotaki or Moore apparent from the profile. The profile does not state any connection to Gertler, whose appearance on the B012 and B007 credit lists I note only for attribution.
